title: System design for interviews
goal: Pass junior-to-mid system-design interviews as a full-stack (React/Next/Node/NestJS) engineer: structure a 45-minute design, reason about trade-offs, and deliver a working system for common prompts

nodes.title: Back-of-envelope estimation
nodes.why: Numbers (QPS, storage, bandwidth) justify every later choice: one box or many, cache or not, shard or not
focus: latency numbers and powers of two
QPS and peak QPS from daily active users
when estimation changes a design decision
outcomes: estimate average and peak QPS, 5-year storage and bandwidth for a feature within 2x in 5 minutes
use an estimate to decide whether a component needs to scale out, and say why
rank memory, SSD, same-datacenter and cross-region latencies by order of magnitude

nodes.title: Scaling the web tier: DNS, load balancers, CDN
nodes.why: Every design diagram starts with client -> DNS -> load balancer -> stateless app servers; this is the 'zero to millions' backbone
focus: request flow from DNS to server
vertical vs horizontal scaling and stateless servers
CDN push vs pull for static assets
single points of failure and redundancy
outcomes: draw the request path for a web app and name what each hop does
explain why session state must leave the app server before scaling out, and where it goes
choose L4 vs L7 load balancing and push vs pull CDN for a given scenario and justify it
spot single points of failure in a diagram and remove them

nodes.title: Caching strategies
nodes.why: Caching is the first answer to read-heavy load in almost every prompt; interviewers probe invalidation and failure modes

nodes.title: Databases: data modeling and SQL vs NoSQL
nodes.why: Picking and modeling the store (relational, document, key-value, wide-column) is a decision in every design

nodes.title: Replication and sharding
nodes.why: Read replicas and partitioning are how the data layer scales; consistent hashing and hot keys are standard follow-ups

nodes.title: Consistency, CAP and availability
nodes.why: Non-functional requirements are stated as consistency vs availability trade-offs; failover and availability numbers back them up

nodes.title: The system-design interview delivery framework
nodes.why: A fixed track (requirements, entities, API, high-level design, deep dives) is the most common thing mid-level candidates lack and the fastest way to cut interview anxiety
focus: what interviewers assess at junior/mid vs senior level
outcomes: turn a vague prompt into 3 prioritized functional and 3 quantified non-functional requirements in 5 minutes
walk a simple prompt through every framework step within its time box in a 45-minute mock
name the four rubric areas and what a mid-level candidate is expected to show in each

nodes.title: Design a URL shortener
nodes.why: The classic first prompt: read-heavy, small data model, key generation; integrates framework, estimation, caching and DB choice

nodes.title: Message queues and async processing
nodes.why: Queues and pub/sub decouple slow work, absorb spikes and fan out events; needed by chat, notifications and feeds

nodes.title: API design and real-time communication
nodes.why: Choosing REST/gRPC/GraphQL, pagination, idempotency, rate limiting, and polling vs SSE vs WebSocket shows up in every API step

nodes.title: Design a chat system
nodes.why: Builds on the learner's WebSocket background: connection servers, message fan-out across servers, storage and ordering

nodes.title: Design a notification system
nodes.why: Queue-driven delivery to push/SMS/email with retries, deduplication and user preferences; a second practice prompt for queues and APIs that nothing later depends on, so it can be skipped under a short deadline

nodes.title: Design a news feed
nodes.why: Fan-out on write vs read, feed caching and celebrity hot keys: the integrating prompt for caching, sharding, queues and eventual consistency

milestones.title: The data layer and the interview framework
